meaning.text: When the domovoy haunts a bath (banya), he is known as a Bannik.
Because the domovoy also settles in bath-houses, wherever a stove is built, he is given the name bannyi (bannik).

scene.text: His whistling, laughter and howling are often heard from behind the stove or from under the sweating-shelf of the bath-house.

behavior_habitat.text: Lives behind the stove or under the sweating-shelf (polok) of the bath-house.
Does not like people who bathe (steam themselves) at night.
Often suffocates those who bathe at night, especially if they have not prefaced their washing with a prayer.

dealing_with_it.text: The peasants avoid visiting the bath at late hours.
In the Smolensk Government, peasants who leave the bath leave a bucket of water and a whisk (besom) for the domovoy who takes their place, so that he too can wash and steam himself.
In the Smolensk Government, when climbing onto the sweating-shelf to steam, people say: "The baptised onto the shelf, the unbaptised off the shelf!"

origin.text: Besides the hut, the domovoy settles in bath-houses, corn-drying barns and distilleries, in a word wherever a stove is built.

Afanasyev writes that when the wish for greater comfort led people to build separate bath-houses and corn-drying barns, the domovoy received new names, and these names gave rise to the idea of special spirits in charge of these outbuildings.

rationale.text: The only people named in the verified entry is the Russians (one general row and one Smolensk Government row).
Afanasyev names the bannik as the domovoy living in the bath-house and gives its haunts, sounds, night-time suffocation and the Smolensk shelf saying and bucket-and-whisk custom.
Ralston names the Bannik as the domovoy haunting the bath and gives the night-bathing danger and the Smolensk bucket-and-whisk custom; his bannik passage cites and quotes no source.

Ralston cites Afanasyev two pages earlier for a different domovoy custom (footnote 8, "Afanasief, P. V. S. ii. 67"), not for the bannik passage, so under the per-passage rule the two are counted as two independent sources; his p.123 passage nevertheless follows the order and details of Afanasyev p.69 closely.
One people with two independent authors grades regional.

notes.text: appearance: no source describes the bannik's body, size, hair, clothing or any form it takes; searched bannik, bannilc, banya, bath, bath-room, банник, банникъ, баннаго, банный, банн, баня, банѣ, бане, банях, подовинник across all sources (bath scoped to ralston1872, ralston1873, machal1918). Only ralston1872 p.123 and afanasyev1868 pp.69-70 name the bannik, and neither describes him.
variants: no source distinguishes the bannik by people or region; only Russians are named, and the Smolensk detail is a custom, not a different description. Same searches as for appearance.

Both naming sources present the bannik as the domovoy when he lives in the bath (ralston1872 p.123, afanasyev1868 p.69), and Ralston's and Afanasyev's Smolensk bucket-and-whisk custom is written as being for 'the domovoy' in the bath; it is kept here because each page ties it to the bath spirit in the same passage. Two further pages speak of the domovoy or domestic spirits in the bath-house without naming the bannik and were left out under the narrow-attribution rule: machal1918 p.241 (the domovoy in the bath-room creeps under the benches, hissing, rumbling and giggling; a pail of water is made ready for him) and afanasyev1869 p.310 (in Novgorod Government the stealing of infants is ascribed to domestic spirits living in bath-houses, where women after childbirth are taken to be washed). The verify agent or Ben may decide whether these belong here or under domovoi.

names.variants: 'bannago' is a plain transliteration of the form printed in afanasyev1868 p.69 ('баннаго', genitive in the phrase 'названія баннаго (банника)'); the page does not print a nominative of this name. The Ralston variant 'Bannik' is the English-text spelling (OCR also renders it 'Bannilc' on the same page).

Editorial: physical descriptions of the bannik and other bath-house lore found in modern games, fiction and internet sources are excluded; this entry records only what the two cited 19th-century pages say, and neither describes his appearance.
